specPoints.text: describe how thermal energy transfer may take place by conduction, convection and radiation
explain the role of convection in everyday phenomena
explain how emission and absorption of radiation are related to surface and temperature

primer.text: Heating moves energy three ways: through solids by colliding particles (conduction, turbocharged in metals by delocalised electrons), through fluids by density-driven currents (convection), and through nothing at all by infrared waves (radiation). The surface and the state of matter decide which route wins.

lessons.title: Conduction, conductors and insulators
sourceHeadings: Example of a conductor and an insulator
lessons.opening: Conduction is the main route by which heating moves energy through solids. Metals conduct superbly; non-metals, liquids and gases barely conduct at all — and the poor conductors earn a name of their own, insulators, which is exactly what you want under your feet on a cold bathroom floor.
keyPoints: Conduction moves heating energy through solids by particle jostling.
Metals are extremely good thermal conductors.
Non-metals conduct poorly, and liquids and gases barely conduct at all.
Poor conductors are called insulators, and they prevent energy transfer by conduction.
Materials containing pockets of trapped air are especially good insulators because air is a gas and cannot form convection currents when trapped.

low.restatement: Solids conduct by particle collisions; metals do it best, gases barely at all, and trapped air is the reason fluffy materials insulate so well.
low.analogy: A queue passing buckets hand to hand: a tight queue (solid) passes fast, a scattered crowd (gas) barely passes at all.
low.examPointer: Name the mechanism in answers: heated particles vibrate harder and knock into neighbours, handing energy along.

medium.restatement: The conductor-insulator split is a spectrum: metals at the top, non-metal solids far below, liquids lower still and gases lowest — which is why materials that trap air are the designers’ favourite insulators.
medium.analogy: Rumour spreading in an office (tight desks, fast) versus a city park (people far apart, slow): closeness sets the transfer rate.
medium.examPointer: Trapped-air answers need BOTH halves: air is a poor conductor AND it is trapped so it cannot move to form a convection current.

check.stem: Which process carries heating energy through solids?

options.explanation: Convection needs a fluid; it cannot happen in solids.
Conduction is the main heating transfer route in solids.
Radiation passes through, but conduction dominates in solids.
Evaporation is a change of state, not the solid heating route.

check.stem: Which group of materials conducts heat best?

options.explanation: Gases are extremely poor conductors.
Metals are extremely good thermal conductors.
Liquids are poor conductors.
Non-metals are poor conductors.

check.stem: What makes a material a good insulator?

options.explanation: That describes a conductor.

options.text: does not transfer energy by heating
options.explanation: Insulators stop the conduction route.
Free electrons belong to metals and speed conduction.
Metals are the best conductors, not insulators.

check.stem: Why is trapped air such a good insulator?

options.explanation: Nothing absorbs and destroys energy.

options.text: air is a gas, so it conducts very slowly, and when trapped it cannot move to form convection currents
options.explanation: Both halves make trapped air special.

options.text: air reflects heat like a mirror
options.explanation: Reflection is the shiny-surface behaviour for radiation.

options.text: air has no particles at all
options.explanation: Air is full of particles; they are just far apart.

check.stem: Why does conduction pull energy from bare feet faster through tiles than through a rug?

options.text: the tiles are colder than the rug
options.explanation: Both sit at room temperature.

options.text: the tiles conduct energy from the feet faster than the rug does
options.explanation: Better conduction pulls heat from the feet faster, so tiles feel colder.

options.text: the rug heats the feet by radiation
options.explanation: The rug insulates; it does not actively heat.
The rug has no energy source.

check.stem: State what poor conductors are called.
check.modelAnswer: Poor conductors are called insulators — materials that do not transfer energy by heating.

check.stem: State what happens to the atoms of a substance when it is heated.
check.modelAnswer: Heated atoms vibrate harder, knock into their neighbours and hand energy along from atom to atom.

check.stem: Explain why a woolly hat keeps a head warm even though wool itself is not a heat source.
check.modelAnswer: Wool traps air in small pockets. The air is a gas, so it conducts heat away from the head very slowly, and because the air is trapped it cannot circulate to carry energy off by convection either — so the head loses energy to the surroundings much more slowly.

check.stem: A saucepan has a metal body and a plastic handle. Explain the choice of material for each part.
check.modelAnswer: The body is metal because conduction must transfer energy from the hob to the food quickly; the handle is plastic because conduction into the hand must be slow, and plastics are poor conductors — good insulators.

lessons.title: How conduction works, and why metals win
lessons.opening: Heat one end of a solid and its atoms vibrate harder, jostling their neighbours and passing energy along atom by atom. Metals add a second delivery service: their delocalised electrons roam freely and collide with atoms, carrying the vibrations — and the heat — far faster than the lattice alone could.
keyPoints: Heating makes a substance’s atoms vibrate harder and knock into their neighbours.
Each collision passes energy from atom to atom through the material.
Metals contain delocalised electrons that can move through the lattice.
The delocalised electrons collide with atoms and help transfer the vibrations through the metal.
This extra transfer mechanism is why metals conduct heat better than non-metals.

low.restatement: Two mechanisms: the lattice passes vibrations by collision, and in metals the free electrons ferry energy between atoms, which is the metals’ winning edge.
low.analogy: Passing a message down a line of people by shoulder taps, while in a metal some runners also sprint along the queue carrying copies.
low.examPointer: The phrase that scores: delocalised electrons collide with atoms, transferring the vibrations through the material faster.

medium.restatement: Particle picture: heating raises the vibration amplitude of lattice atoms; collisions propagate it; electron collisions add a fast parallel channel unique to metals.
medium.analogy: A crowded standing wave at a concert: the push of neighbour on neighbour spreads the sway, and the stewards moving through the crowd spread it faster still.
medium.examPointer: Do not say electrons carry heat like a fluid — say they collide with atoms and transfer energy, which is the model’s actual claim.

check.stem: When one end of a metal rod is heated, how does energy reach the far end?

options.text: the hot atoms travel along the rod
options.explanation: Atoms stay in place; only energy travels.

options.text: atoms vibrate more and pass energy on through collisions, helped by delocalised electrons
options.explanation: Both mechanisms carry the energy.

options.text: the rod melts gradually from the hot end
options.explanation: Melting is a change of state, not conduction.

options.text: infra-red light carries the energy inside the rod
options.explanation: Radiation is not the internal route here.

check.stem: What special particles do metals contain that non-metals lack, speeding conduction?

options.explanation: Protons are bound in nuclei in every solid.
Neutrons stay in nuclei everywhere.
Metals’ free electrons collide with atoms and speed the transfer.
The lattice is atoms, not free neutrons.

check.stem: Why does the lattice alone conduct more slowly than a metal’s full mechanism?

options.explanation: Vibration is exactly what they do.

options.text: collision-to-collision transfer through the lattice is slower than the extra electron collisions
options.explanation: Electrons add a faster parallel route.
Non-metals have atoms; they lack free electrons.
Temperature is the condition, not the mechanism.

check.stem: A metal spoon in hot soup becomes too hot to hold while a wooden spoon does not. The key difference is:

options.explanation: Wood is solid; the difference is the material, not a hole.

options.text: metal’s delocalised electrons conduct the soup’s energy up the handle quickly
options.explanation: Fast conduction is the metal’s behaviour.
Absorption of liquid is not the thermal point here.

options.text: metal has a lower melting point
options.explanation: Nothing melts in this scenario.

check.stem: Which row correctly orders conduction speed through the same shape of bar?

options.text: copper bar > plastic bar > air gap
options.explanation: Metal, then non-metal solid, then gas — fastest to slowest.

options.text: air gap > copper bar > plastic bar
options.explanation: Air is the worst conductor of the three.

options.text: plastic bar > copper bar > air gap
options.explanation: Metal beats plastic.
The material decides the rate.

check.stem: State what the delocalised electrons in a metal do to help thermal conduction.
check.modelAnswer: They crash into the metal’s atoms, handing the vibrations along through the material, which moves heat faster.

check.stem: State what happens to the spacing of particles in a material that is very dense, and its effect on conduction.
check.modelAnswer: Denser materials pack their particles nearer together, so the collision chain passes energy along more easily.

check.stem: Explain why a metal chain feels colder than a rope left overnight in the same cold shed.
check.modelAnswer: Both sit at the shed’s temperature, but the metal’s delocalised electrons conduct energy from your warm hand into the chain far faster than the rope’s non-metal lattice does, so the chain drains heat from the hand quickly and feels colder.

check.stem: A soldering iron tip is copper but its handle is wood-effect plastic. Use conduction to explain both choices.
check.modelAnswer: The copper tip must deliver heat to the joint quickly, and copper’s delocalised electrons make it an excellent conductor; the plastic handle must not conduct that heat to the grip, and being a poor conductor it insulates the user’s hand.

lessons.title: Convection and convection currents
lessons.opening: Fluids — liquids and gases — carry heat by moving themselves: convection. Warm fluid expands, becomes less dense than its surroundings, and rises; cooler fluid sinks into its place; the cycle draws a convection current. Solids are excluded — nothing flows — which is why the mechanism belongs to fluids alone.
keyPoints: Convection moves thermal energy through fluids — liquids and gases — by bulk flow of the fluid itself.
Convection cannot occur in solids.
When a fluid is heated, its particles push apart and the fluid expands.
The hot fluid is less dense than its surroundings, so it rises.
Cooler fluid moves in to take its place; the hot fluid cools, contracts and sinks, forming a convection current.

low.restatement: Heat a fluid, it expands and floats upward; cool fluid replaces it and the loop repeats — a convection current that shuttles energy through the fluid bulk.
low.analogy: A warm-air balloon: heated air lifts the basket because expansion made it lighter per cubic metre than the air around it.
low.examPointer: Convection answers need the density chain: heated → expands → less dense → rises; and the replacement step: cooler fluid sinks in to take its place.

medium.restatement: The current is a closed loop driven by density differences: rise above the heat source, lose energy to the surroundings at the top, contract, sink, and return to be heated again.
medium.analogy: An escalator pair in a shopping centre: one side carries warm air up, the other returns the cooled flow down, and the loop never stops while the heater works.
medium.examPointer: Everyday phenomena to quote: sea breezes, radiators warming a room, boiling water’s rolling motion.

check.stem: In which states of matter can convection occur?

options.explanation: Solids cannot flow, so no convection.
Convection needs a fluid; solids are excluded.
Liquids convect too — boiling water is the classic case.
Metals are solids; they conduct instead.

check.stem: Why does heated fluid rise?

options.text: it weighs less because heating destroys particles
options.explanation: Particles are conserved; heating only spreads them.

options.text: heating makes the fluid expand, so it becomes less dense than the surrounding fluid
options.explanation: Lower density floats above higher density.
The current forms even with gentle heating.
Particles move APART when heated.

check.stem: What completes a convection current after the hot fluid rises?

options.text: the fluid stays at the top forever
options.explanation: It cools at the top and returns.

options.text: the hot fluid cools, contracts, becomes denser and sinks back down
options.explanation: The sinking return leg closes the loop.

options.text: the fluid evaporates at the top
options.explanation: Evaporation is not part of the current cycle.

options.text: the fluid turns solid at the top
options.explanation: Nothing freezes in a convection current demonstration.

check.stem: A radiator warms a room mainly through which transfer process — conduction, convection or radiation?

options.text: conduction through the air, because air conducts well
options.explanation: Air conducts very poorly.

options.text: convection: warm air rises from the radiator, cools and circulates
options.explanation: The room-wide circulation is a convection current.
Radiation contributes, but the room-wide warming is convective.
Condensation is a change of state, not the warming route.

check.stem: Why does a sea breeze blow from the sea towards the land on a hot day? Answer using convection.

options.text: the land heats the air above it, which rises, and cooler air from the sea moves in to replace it
options.explanation: The land-side updraught pulls the sea breeze ashore.

options.text: the sea heats the air above it, which rises towards the land
options.explanation: Water heats slowly; the land is the hot side.

options.text: the wind is caused by waves pushing air
options.explanation: Waves are a result of wind, not its cause.

options.text: cold air rises from the sea
options.explanation: Cold air sinks.

check.stem: State what happens to the density of a fluid when it is heated, and the immediate effect.
check.modelAnswer: Heated fluid expands, becoming less dense than the surroundings, so it rises.

check.stem: State why convection cannot happen in a solid.
check.modelAnswer: Convection needs the fluid itself to flow; solids cannot flow, so convection cannot occur in them.

check.stem: Explain why a room warms better if the heater is placed near the floor rather than near the ceiling.
check.modelAnswer: Warm air rises, so a floor-level heater starts its convection current through the whole room’s height: warm air climbs, cools against the ceiling and walls, and sinks back to be reheated. A ceiling-level heater warms only the top layer, which is already above the cooler air and so barely circulates.

check.stem: A pan of water is heated gently at one side and a crystal of potassium permanganate sits above the flame. Describe what the purple trail shows.
check.modelAnswer: The purple trail rises with the warmed water above the flame, spreads across the surface, cools, sinks at the far side and returns along the bottom to the flame — tracing the closed loop of the convection current.

lessons.title: Thermal radiation and the mug of coffee
sourceHeadings: Conduction, convection and radiation in a mug of coffee
lessons.opening: Every object, whatever its temperature, emits infrared radiation — no particles, no medium, just waves. Hotter objects radiate more per second, and the surface decides how well: black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers, shiny surfaces the worst. A cooling mug of coffee runs all three transfer routes at once.
keyPoints: All bodies emit infrared radiation, whatever their temperature.
A hotter object radiates more infrared in a given time.
Black objects are the best emitters and absorbers of thermal radiation; shiny objects are the worst.
Shiny surfaces reflect radiation, which is why they absorb so poorly.
A hot mug of coffee loses energy by radiation from its surfaces, by conduction through the mug walls, and by convection of the warm air above it.

low.restatement: Radiation is the no-medium route: every object emits infrared, hotter means more, and the surface’s colour and finish set the emit-absorb score, black best and shiny worst.
low.analogy: A spotlight that every object shines all the time, turned up by temperature; the surface is the lampshade, black glass letting everything through, polished metal bouncing it back.
low.examPointer: The mug-of-coffee question wants all three routes named with their surfaces: radiation from the surface, conduction through the walls, convection above the drink.

medium.restatement: Emission and absorption are two sides of the same surface quality: good absorbers are good emitters (black, dull), poor absorbers are poor emitters (white, shiny — shiny reflects instead).
medium.analogy: A good listener is usually a good talker: surfaces that take radiation in easily also give it out easily; the mirror-finish ones do neither.
medium.examPointer: Sort the four surfaces in order when asked: black > dull/dark > white > shiny, for BOTH absorbing and emitting.

check.stem: What does every object do, whatever its temperature?

options.explanation: Every object also EMITS.
All bodies emit infrared all the time.
Convection needs a fluid; not every object is fluid.
Conduction needs contact; radiation needs nothing.

check.stem: How does temperature affect the radiation an object emits?

options.explanation: It is the other way round.

options.text: the hotter the object, the more infrared it radiates in a given time
options.explanation: Emission rate rises with temperature.

options.text: temperature has no effect on emission
options.explanation: Temperature is the driver of emission rate.

options.text: only very hot objects emit any radiation
options.explanation: All bodies emit, however cool.

check.stem: Which surface is the best absorber AND emitter of thermal radiation?

options.explanation: Shiny is the worst at both — it reflects.
White is a poor absorber and emitter.
Black surfaces are the best at emitting and absorbing.
The surface quality decides.

check.stem: A thermos flask keeps drinks hot partly by coating surfaces with shiny metal. Why does that work?

options.text: shiny metal conducts the heat away faster
options.explanation: The flask wants to STOP transfer, not speed it.

options.text: shiny surfaces are very poor emitters and reflect radiation back, reducing radiated loss
options.explanation: Poor emission plus reflection keeps the radiation in.
Nothing adds energy.

options.text: shiny surfaces stop convection inside the liquid
options.explanation: The coating addresses radiation, not the fluid’s convection.

check.stem: For a mug of hot coffee standing on a table, which loss route does NOT need any material between the coffee and its surroundings?

options.explanation: The mug wall is the material.

options.text: convection of air above the mug
options.explanation: The air is the material.

options.text: radiation from the coffee’s surface and the mug’s outside
options.explanation: Radiation crosses even a vacuum.
Evaporation needs the liquid itself to leave.

check.stem: State how emission and absorption depend on the colour of a surface.
check.modelAnswer: Black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers; shiny surfaces are the worst at both, reflecting radiation instead.

check.stem: State the three routes by which a hot mug of coffee loses energy to the surroundings.
check.modelAnswer: Radiation from its surfaces, conduction through the mug walls, and convection of the warm air above it.

check.stem: Explain why painting a car’s radiator fins matte black helps it cool the engine.
check.modelAnswer: Matte black surfaces are the best emitters of thermal radiation, so the fins radiate the engine’s energy away at the fastest rate the surface allows; being good absorbers too does no harm, because the fins are hotter than their surroundings and the net flow is outward.

check.stem: Two identical mugs of coffee stand on a table, one matte black and one shiny steel. State which cools faster and name the route that differs most between them.
check.modelAnswer: The matte black mug cools faster: it is the better emitter, so the radiation route — the one that needs no medium — carries energy away from it more quickly than from the shiny mug, which reflects and poorly emits.

glossary.definition: Energy transfer by heating through particle collisions, the main route in solids.
A poor conductor that does not transfer energy by heating well; trapped-air materials are the classic case.
Free electrons in metals that collide with atoms and speed up thermal conduction.
The closed loop of a heated fluid: hot fluid rises, cools, contracts and sinks back.
Infrared emission that every object gives out, needing no medium; black surfaces emit and absorb best.
